books.section: Topic 9.3 The End of the Cold War
Prosperity and a New World Order (1988-2000)

options.misconception: The Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, so it could not veto American actions during the 1990s.
options.text: The Soviet Union threatened to veto every American action in the United Nations

options.misconception: No law required yearly troop deployments; each intervention was a separate decision.
options.text: Congress passed a law requiring the president to send troops abroad each year
With the Soviet Union gone, no rival power could check American action abroad

options.misconception: Background: the United States stayed in NATO after the Cold War; it did not withdraw.
options.text: The United States had withdrawn from NATO and needed new allies

rationales.A: The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991. It could not block American actions during the 1990s.
rationales.B: No law required yearly troop deployments. Each intervention in the 1990s was a separate decision.
rationales.C: The account says the United States stood alone as the only superpower, with no rival to stand in the way of action.
rationales.D: Background: the United States stayed in NATO after the Cold War ended. It did not withdraw.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what had changed about the world by the 1990s.
2. The account says the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, leaving the United States as the only superpower.
3. Background: during the Cold War, the fear of a Soviet response had limited American action.
4. Once that check was gone, each new crisis raised the question of acting, and the United States often did.
Remember: when a check on power disappears, watch for that power to be used more often.

stem: Which of the following most directly explains why the United States intervened in several conflicts during the 1990s?

stimulus.source_note: Secondary account paraphrased from the grounding books (Barron's Premium 2027 Ch. 11; 5 Steps 2024 Ch. 29).
stimulus.text:
Paraphrase of a secondary account: When the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991, the United States stood alone as the world's only superpower. The long rivalry that had shaped every American foreign-policy choice since 1945 was gone. In the 1990s, American forces fought Iraq in the Persian Gulf in 1991, joined a humanitarian mission in Somalia in 1992, and led NATO bombing campaigns in Bosnia in 1995 and in Kosovo in 1999.

At the same time, former Communist states in Eastern Europe opened their economies to world markets, and new trade agreements linked more countries together. No rival power now stood in the way of American action, and each new crisis raised the same question: whether the United States should act abroad or stay out.
